Learning Objectives

Color-emphasis rule for this lecture
Colored text in the handout is treated as intentional emphasis. Blue concepts are carried forward as priority facts, while purple callouts preserve specific emphasis or de-emphasis. Full handout pages are not reproduced here; only diagram portions are shown.
LO 1. Discuss amino acid classification based on physical and nutritional properties.
LO 2. Explain how amino acid R groups shape protein folding, the interactions that stabilize higher-order structure, and the causes/consequences of protein misfolding.
LO 3. Describe Michaelis-Menten kinetics and competitive/noncompetitive inhibition, including effects on Vmax and Km and their appearance on Lineweaver-Burk plots.
LO 4. Explain regulation of enzyme activity, including allosterism, feedback inhibition, and feedforward activation.
LO 5. Discuss the clinical significance of isoenzymes and tissue-specific metabolic regulation.
01Amino-acid classification: organize by R group, nutrition, and metabolic fateLO 1
Classification frame
The handout expects you to be able to classify amino acids by hydrophobicity/hydrophilicity, branched vs linear structure, acidic/basic/neutral character, sulfur- or hydroxyl-containing side chains, nutritional requirement, and metabolic product: glucogenic, ketogenic, or both.
Diagram portion from handout page 1. The table combines essentiality with glucogenic/ketogenic classification. The handout mnemonic for the essential amino acids is PVT TIM HALL.
Must know
Arginine is conditionally essential. The handout emphasizes that demand can exceed synthesis during severe stress/illness, impaired intestinal or renal function, rapid growth, pregnancy/lactation, and selected disease states.
Blue-text emphasis
Histidine has maximal buffering capacity near physiologic pH. The handout contrasts histidine's side-chain pKa with Glu/Asp (~4) and Lys/Arg (~11), which are farther from physiologic pH.
02R groups determine folding, membrane placement, and aggregation riskLO 2

Membrane-spanning helices

The handout emphasizes alpha helices of about 20 amino acids as common membrane-spanning regions in receptors. Their lipid-facing R groups are hydrophobic.

Proline

Proline is an alpha-helix breaker: its cyclic structure introduces a kink, so insertion into a helix can alter secondary/tertiary structure and function.

Soluble proteins

Hydrophobic residues are generally buried in the core, while hydrophilic residues face the aqueous environment.

Membrane proteins

Hydrophobic R groups can face outward toward the lipid bilayer and form hydrophobic interactions with it.

Aqueous folding: nonpolar side chains become buried; polar side chains remain exposed.
Membrane-spanning alpha helix: nonpolar side chains face the lipid tails.
Mutation logic
The handout uses the beta-globin position-6 Glu→Val substitution as the classic example of how one R-group change can promote hemoglobin aggregation. The exam move is to connect side-chain chemistry → altered intermolecular interactions → aggregation/function change.

Denaturation and nonenzymatic glycation

Denaturation disrupts secondary, tertiary, and quaternary structure but not primary structure. The handout lists nonenzymatic chemical modification, oxidation, extreme pH, altered ionic strength, temperature extremes, heavy metals, and solvents as causes.
Do not mix these up
Glycation is nonenzymatic covalent attachment of glucose to amino groups. Glycosylation is enzyme-mediated carbohydrate addition.
Diagram portion from page 3. Glucose modifies hemoglobin without an enzyme, leading through an Amadori rearrangement to glycated hemoglobin.
AGE-RAGE chain
Excess glucose → more glycation → advanced glycation end products (AGEs) → RAGE signaling → NF-kB activation → inflammatory cytokines + reactive oxygen species. The handout describes a self-sustaining damage loop and links it to diabetic vascular/neurologic complications.
Colored-text emphasis
Rate of glycation is proportional to glucose concentration. HbA1c is glucose attached to the N-terminal amino group of the beta chain; it forms over the red-cell lifespan and reflects average glucose over the preceding 2-3 months.

Misfolding, amyloid, and prions

Chaperones promote normal folding. Misfolded proteins can lose activity and form insoluble, protease-resistant, beta-sheet-rich aggregates. The handout calls proteins/genes that commonly form such aggregates amyloidogenic.
PrPC is alpha-helix-rich; infectious PrPSc has much more beta-sheet and is protease resistant.
PrPSc templates conversion of normal PrPC, creating an autocatalytic accumulation cycle.
Prion essentials
Prions are infectious proteins with no DNA or RNA. The conformational change is described as alpha-helix → beta-sheet through disruption/reformation of hydrogen bonds. The handout highlights CJD, GSS, fatal familial insomnia, Kuru, and variant CJD.
Other aggregation diseases named in the handout
Alzheimer disease, Huntington disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (superoxide dismutase I), and Parkinson disease (alpha-synuclein and others). These are described as beta-sheet-rich aggregate diseases but not infectious by ingestion.
03Michaelis-Menten kinetics: what Km and Vmax actually tell youLO 3
Core equations in words
Km = substrate concentration at 1/2 Vmax. Low Km = high affinity. High Km = low affinity. Km does not change when enzyme concentration changes. Vmax is directly proportional to enzyme concentration.
Michaelis-Menten kinetics are hyperbolic; Km is read at 1/2 Vmax.
Double reciprocal plot: x-intercept = -1/Km; y-intercept = 1/Vmax.
ConditionBehavior emphasized in the handout
[S] much less than KmVelocity is proportional to substrate concentration: first-order with respect to substrate.
[S] much greater than KmVelocity is constant at Vmax: zero-order with respect to substrate.
More enzymeVmax increases; Km stays the same.
Enzyme denaturation / loss of expression / loss-of-functionVmax changes because effective enzyme amount changes.
One enzyme, multiple substratesThe substrate with the lowest Km is used first.
Foundational distinction
Enzymes lower activation energy; the handout explicitly reminds you that they do not change the reaction's Gibbs free-energy change (ΔG).
04Enzyme inhibition: binding site → reversibility → Km/Vmax patternLO 3
TypeWhere/How it bindsVmaxKmCan more substrate overcome?
CompetitiveActive site; free enzyme onlyUnchangedIncreasedYes
NoncompetitiveDistinct site; can bind E or ESDecreasedUnchangedNo
IrreversibleCovalent or extremely tight bindingDecreasedApparent Km unchanged in the handoutNo
Diagram-only excerpt from page 8. Compare binding model, direct plot, and double-reciprocal pattern rather than memorizing isolated arrows.

Competitive clinical examples

Ethylene glycol/methanol metabolism and use of ethanol when fomepizole is unavailable; sulfa drugs competing with PABA-related folate synthesis.

Noncompetitive examples in this handout

AMP inhibition of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and morphine inhibition of nitric oxide synthase.

Irreversible and suicide inhibition

The handout names irreversible inhibition by covalent modification, including disulfiram inhibition of aldehyde dehydrogenase and organophosphate inhibition of acetylcholinesterase. Increased acetylcholine at the motor endplate can produce persistent depolarization and paralysis.
Penicillin is presented as a suicide substrate/inhibitor: the transpeptidase activates the beta-lactam during catalysis, and penicillin then covalently modifies the active-site serine.
Fast recognition
Competitive = active site, Km up, Vmax same. Noncompetitive = other site, Vmax down, Km same. Irreversible = functional enzyme amount down, Vmax down.
05Regulating enzyme activity: quantity, cleavage, partners, covalent switches, and allosteryLO 4
Regulatory mechanismExample from the handout
Synthesis/degradationAlter protein abundance through gene expression or degradation.
Limited proteolysisPancreatic enzymes secreted as zymogens.
Protein-protein interactionLipoprotein lipase-apoCII interaction.
Reversible covalent modificationPKA-dependent phosphorylation regulates glycogen synthase and glycogen phosphorylase in opposite directions.
Allosteric regulationReversible effector binding at a site other than the active site can stimulate or inhibit activity.
Feedforward: an early metabolite activates a downstream enzyme.
Feedback: the end product inhibits the first enzyme of the pathway.
Allosteric enzyme pattern
Most allosteric enzymes are multimeric and have quaternary structure. Their velocity-vs-substrate plot is sigmoidal rather than hyperbolic. The handout emphasizes inhibitor → right shift and activator → left shift.
Michaelis-Menten enzymes give a hyperbolic curve; allosteric enzymes give a sigmoidal curve.

Aspartate transcarbamoylase example

Colored-text priority
This is the handout's classic high-yield allosteric example. The reactants and products in the pathway diagram are explicitly de-emphasized at this stage.
ATP is a positive modulator and shifts the curve left; CTP is a feedback inhibitor and shifts it right.
The pathway diagram shows CTP end-product feedback and ATP positive regulation. Focus on the regulatory logic, not the de-emphasized reactant/product names.
ATCase one-liner
ATP → left shift → increased apparent substrate affinity. CTP → right shift → decreased apparent substrate affinity.
06Isoenzymes: same reaction, different molecular form, tissue pattern, and diagnostic useLO 5
Isoenzymes catalyze the same reaction but exist in more than one molecular form. The handout emphasizes that they can have different Km/Vmax values and different regulatory sites, but the reaction's equilibrium constant, ΔG, and ΔG° remain unchanged. Activation energy can differ between isoenzymes.
Why serum enzymes can localize injury
When tissue is damaged, intracellular enzymes enter the blood. Tissue-specific isoenzyme expression can therefore help identify which tissue was injured.

Creatine kinase isoenzymes

TissueCK-MBCK-MMCK-BB
Skeletal muscle1%99%0.1%
Heart20%79%1%
Brain3%0%97%

Timing after MI

Total CK is described as rising in 4-12 hours, peaking at about 24 hours, and returning toward normal in 2-3 days.

Specificity logic

Total CK is not cardiac-specific. CK-MB is more specific for cardiac muscle, although some MB is present in skeletal muscle.

Current-practice note included in the handout
The handout explicitly states that CK-MB is rarely used clinically now and that most clinics use cardiac-specific troponin to diagnose cardiac injury.

One-pass recall map

Classify

Essential vs nonessential/conditional; glucogenic vs ketogenic; R-group chemistry; histidine buffering.

Predict folding

Hydrophobic core vs membrane exposure; proline helix break; denaturation vs primary structure.

Read kinetics

Km = 1/2 Vmax; low Km = high affinity; Vmax tracks enzyme amount; first-order vs zero-order substrate regimes.

Discriminate inhibition

Competitive vs noncompetitive vs irreversible by binding site, substrate rescue, Km, and Vmax.

Recognize regulation

Feedback, feedforward, allosteric sigmoidal curves, ATP/CTP shifts.

Use isoenzymes

Same reaction, different form/tissue; CK-MB timing and the handout's troponin note.

Ozzy checkpoint: click him after you can explain competitive vs noncompetitive inhibition without looking.
